summary:
We built a web tool that compares crop rotations on a real plot of land, both under today's climate and under a projected 2050 climate. For each rotation it shows four things: how much of each crop's water demand rain and soil can cover in each season, how soil organic carbon changes over time, the expected yield and margin, and the risk of seasons that lose money.

NASA data drives the engine. NASA POWER daily weather from 2001 to 2024 feeds a FAO-56 evapotranspiration model and a daily water balance. NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections (ACCESS-CM2 model, SSP2-4.5 scenario) adjust that weather to 2050 conditions. NASA GLDAS and SoilGrids supply the soil texture. Every result comes with a plain-language "why?" that explains how the rotation compares with monoculture, because advisors need arguments they can pass on, not a black-box verdict. An MCP server also lets any AI agent query the same engine.

This matters because in Castilla's rain-fed farmland, water runs short in May–July, exactly when cereals need it most, and projections say this will get worse. Cooperative advisors currently have no tool that brings climate, soil and crop together to support rotation choices that protect soil and water now and in 2050.
details:
Campo 2050 helps a farm advisor choose a crop rotation for a specific field, both for today's climate and for a projected 2050 climate. The user picks a location on a 3D globe, checks or edits the soil data, and compares rotations of wheat, barley, lentil, sunflower, vetch and fallow. Users can also enter their own crop prices and costs, and switch on irrigation.

For each rotation, the engine simulates every season from October to September, day by day:

- Climate: NASA POWER daily weather (2001–2024) feeds FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration and a daily soil-water balance.

- 2050 scenario: NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 monthly changes in temperature and rainfall (ACCESS-CM2 model, SSP2-4.5) are applied to the historical weather, and evapotranspiration is recalculated.

- Soil: soil texture comes from NASA GLDAS (0.25° grid, stored in the repo so lookups are instant) and organic matter from ISRIC SoilGrids.

- Model: crop development, water stress, yield, soil organic carbon and gross margin.

Rotations are ranked by a weighted score covering water, soil, income and stability. Each result comes with a plain-language "why?" that compares it with monoculture. Results can be exported as a PDF or Markdown report.

Benefits

- Brings climate, soil and crop data together in one place. Advisors currently have no tool that does this.

- Shows today and 2050 side by side, so users can see which rotations hold up under a drier, hotter future.

- Explains each result, which gives advisors arguments they can pass on to farmers rather than an unexplained verdict.

- An optional AI advisor answers questions about the field using the engine's results and FAO/NASA sources. It cites only sources it was actually given and states what data is missing.

- An open MCP server (/api/mcp) lets any AI agent query climate, soil, projections and rotation simulations with the same engine.

Intended impact

The aim is rotations that protect soil and water in rain-fed areas such as Castilla, where water runs short in May–July, exactly when cereals need it, and projections say this will get worse. Picking rotations with legumes or fallow that keep soil carbon up and lower the risk of loss-making seasons helps farms adapt before the shortage becomes severe.

Tools and technologies

- Languages: TypeScript, with Python for preprocessing the GLDAS grid.

- Web app: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4.

- Visuals: Three.js and React Three Fiber for the 3D Earth and field scenes, Recharts for charts, Motion for animation.

- Validation and AI: Zod for data validation; Model Context Protocol SDK for the MCP server; an AI advisor with retrieval that works with Gemini, Groq or OpenAI.

- Testing and hosting: Vitest and the Node test runner; deployed on Vercel.

- Data: NASA POWER, NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, NASA GLDAS, ISRIC SoilGrids, FAO-56.

- Testing and hosting: Vitest and the Node test runner; deployed on Vercel.

- Data: NASA POWER, NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, NASA GLDAS, ISRIC SoilGrids, FAO-56.

- Hardware: none; it runs entirely in the browser and the cloud.

What makes it creative

- It turns NASA climate projections into a practical farm decision ("which rotation?") rather than just a climate map.

- The "why?" explanations are written for a human advisor.

- The same engine serves people through the website and AI agents through MCP.

- The 3D globe-to-field journey makes the data concrete for non-specialists.

Factors the team considered

- Honesty about uncertainty: 2050 is labelled as a possible scenario, not a forecast, because it rests on one climate model. Every value keeps its data source, and fallback or demo values are labelled as such.

- Scientific basis: FAO-56 equations, documented crop assumptions and unit tests on the equations.

- The real user: a cooperative advisor who needs editable soil data, prices and costs, and a report to share.

- Reliability: cached data and stored snapshots let it keep working when external services are slow. It works on mobile, and the core engine needs no AI keys.

- Known limits and next steps: compare the water balance against NASA SMAP soil moisture, use a set of climate models instead of one, and calibrate crop parameters locally.
